description: Student replication of post-earnings-announcement drift (Bernard-Thomas) conditioned on Google Trends investor attention (Da-Engelberg-Gao) and same-day earnings congestion (Hirshleifer-Lim-Teoh), for 16 US mega-caps (no ABNB). Source: yfinance earnings dates/prices and manual Google Trends CSV downloads (a download plan and naming convention are committed, but no pull dates). For ABNB, the value is the scaffold - the event-study code and the drift-by-attention/distraction base rates (drift +0.7% low-distraction vs -1.1% high-distraction, n=238) can be re-run on ABNB's 5 Nov print and its 2020-2026 event history; the Trends pull plan is a template, not point-in-time provenance.
issues: No LICENSE file - reuse rights undetermined (tos_or_license_flag). Google Trends CSVs were downloaded manually via the browser UI; the instructions give settings (US, past 5y, web search) but NOT the pull date, so the attention panel is a single vintage, not point-in-time (gap #4 only partly served). Data covers 16 mega-caps, no ABNB or travel names; earnings dates come from yfinance and are not independently verified. Small n (238 merged events) makes the drift base rates indicative only. description: Booking.com's official WSDM WebTour 2021 challenge release: 1.55M anonymised real hotel reservations (2016 to Feb 2017) grouped into multi-destination trips, one row per reservation with check-in/check-out dates, anonymised city and country IDs (countries carry fictional names such as Gondal, Elbonia), device class, affiliate channel and booker country. Grain is reservation within trip; source is Booking.com itself, hosted ungated on HuggingFace. An ABNB analyst would use it as a competitor base rate for length-of-stay distributions (head: mean 1.74 nights, median 1), share of cross-border stays (~90% in the head, which is biased because the challenge selects multi-city trips), device mix and trip-chaining behaviour, not as a nowcast input given the 2016 vintage.
issues: Licence CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0: non-commercial and no-derivatives; a competition pitch is arguably non-commercial but a human should confirm before quoting figures. Country and city identifiers are anonymised (fictional country names, integer city IDs) so no real geography or regional split can be recovered; no price, room type or accommodation type column, so no ADR or STR/hotel split. README lists a created_date column that is absent from the files (no lead-time measure). Heads are the first N bytes of files sorted by user_id, so booker_country shows only 5 values in the head; the ground_truth file was pulled in full. Sample is multi-city trips only (4+ reservations per trip), so LOS and cross-border shares are not representative of all Booking.com bookings.

Sampling caveat: guest_country is anonymised (codes like 'Zuc'), the sample is 2023 only, reviews were filtered to 'informative' ones with >=3 topics and only tens of thousands of properties, so shares are not population estimates. description: Booking.com search-result listings captured by Bright Data (a commercial scraper vendor) and published on HuggingFace: one row per property returned for a search (city/region, check-in date, adults, rooms) with quoted final_price vs original_price in USD, free-cancellation and no-prepayment flags, cancellation deadline, bedroom/bed/kitchen counts, review score and count, and sustainability JSON. Grain is listing x search; check-ins are six dates from 27 Dec 2024 to 27 Feb 2025, so it is a one-off cross-section, not a time series; the head spans 50 country codes (India, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, US, Vietnam, Thailand, Italy lead). For ABNB an analyst would use it as a competitor-pricing and payment-terms backdrop: the share of Booking.com inventory offered with no prepayment (39% in the head; free_cancellation is 100% in the head, so the capture was probably filtered on that flag) and the discount depth (29% of rows discounted, median 22%) frame the RNPL / cancellation thesis, and nb_bedrooms > 0 (31% of rows) isolates alternative-accommodation units for a capacity/party-size comparison against Inside Airbnb.
issues: Licence is 'other' = Bright Data Master Service Agreement, not an open licence; the CSV is world-readable without a token but redistribution rights are unclear, so only a 5 MB head was taken and the remaining ~58 MB was NOT fetched pending a human licence decision (tos_or_license_flag=true). Data provenance is a scraper vendor's marketing sample, one-off cross-section with a 100% free_cancellation share (likely a filtered search), so cancellation shares are not representative of all Booking.com inventory. Eight columns (country, hotel_rank, searched_country, map_coordinates, listing_country, total_listings_found, star_rating, tags) are entirely null in the head; listing country was recovered from the /hotel/<cc>/ path in url instead. One row priced in BRL, the rest USD. No scraper was run; no airbnb.com contact.

description: Weekly point-in-time snapshots of the sell-side analyst revenue (sales_estimate) and EPS (eps_estimate) consensus per ticker and forecast period (current/next quarter, current/next year), with contributor count, high, low and year-ago value, plus an earnings-date calendar and EPS actual history; Zacks-style schema, published as a public Dolt database by DoltHub user post-no-preference. Grain: one row per (snapshot date, ticker, period). For ABNB the sample holds the complete revenue-consensus history from 2021-02-07 to 2026-09-13 (1,160 rows), so an analyst can reconstruct what the Street expected at every guide date and print in the guidance ledger, measure consensus drift and dispersion into each print (e.g. 4Q26 revenue $3.20bn mean, $3.05-3.70bn range, n=10 as of 2026-09-13), and register it as a second, timestamped consensus vendor in the L0 vintage register; the same tables cover BKNG and EXPE for peer readthrough.
issues: (1) No licence stated on the DoltHub page; the underlying numbers look like redistributed Zacks consensus data - a human must decide whether it can be quoted or only used internally (tos_or_license_flag=true). (2) The API is fragile: any query touching more than one ticker, any aggregate (count/min/max), and larger offsets frequently return 'context deadline exceeded'; one HTTP 403 (rate limit) appeared after ~40 requests in 20 minutes. BKNG sales_estimate was truncated at 1,000 rows and EXPE, eps_history and the full eps_estimate were not pulled. (3) Estimate values are bigint (whole dollars / EPS in cents-like units for eps? - check: sales consensus 4740000000 = $4.74bn; eps consensus units need confirming against a known print). (4) earnings_calendar shows 23 ABNB dates up to 2026-08-06; the 5 Nov 2026 date is not yet listed. (5) Snapshot dates are Sundays; rows are not present for every week (gaps), so any point-in-time join must use as-of logic.

issues: Licence: code is MIT (Ram Vasuthevan); data is Open Government Licence - Toronto v1.0 (commercial use allowed with attribution 'Contains information licensed under the Open Government Licence - Toronto'); GitHub shows NOASSERTION because the two are combined in one LICENSE file. Registrations are the licensed-to-operate stock, not listings, and 2024-2025 declines may reflect renewal cycles rather than exits; no explicit date column, the first vintage carries an extra _id column; one row in later vintages uses a non-standard property_type label 'Single-family detached'. Nothing failed.

one_line: Small MIT tool ingesting daily Wikimedia Analytics pageviews for 8 NZ attraction pages via the public, keyless Wikimedia API.
abnb_use: Directly fills gap 5 (Wikipedia pageviews tooling) and gap 20 (destination-attention proxy); could be repointed at ABNB-relevant destination or FIFA World Cup host-city pages as a free, point-in-time-able engagement series, unlike our failed Google Trends attempt.
rows: pv_*.json: 105 daily items each (4 files, 420 total); pageviews_daily.csv: 420 rows; venues.csv: 8 rows
geography: Global (en.wikipedia readers); sample articles: Airbnb, Mexico City, Lisbon, Kyoto; repo targets New Zealand attractions
full_dataset_size: The repo itself holds no data (8-row venues.csv + ingest code). The underlying Wikimedia pageviews API covers every Wikipedia article daily/monthly from 2015-07-01 (hourly and per-article endpoints); one article-year is ~50 KB JSON, so a few hundred destination/attraction articles over 11 years is ~100-300 MB JSON (~1.5M rows). description: Daily user (non-spider) pageview counts for English Wikipedia articles, pulled keyless from the public Wikimedia Analytics REST API; one row per article-day. The GitHub repo is a small MIT ingest tool aimed at 8 New Zealand attraction pages and holds no data, so the sample calls the API directly for four ABNB-relevant articles (Airbnb, Mexico_City, Lisbon, Kyoto). An analyst would repoint it at a basket of destination, attraction, and FIFA World Cup 2026 host-city pages to build a free, reproducible destination-attention series back to July 2015 that is not renormalised the way Google Trends is, and test it as a lead on regional nights or as a point-in-time engagement proxy (the Airbnb article itself).

Mexico_City spikes to 59k views on one day (news event), so series need spike-robust treatment. Pageviews are English-Wikipedia only here; other language projects need separate calls. Data start is 2015-07-01 (legacy pagecounts before that are a different basis). Repo has 0 stars and a 4-day-old push; treat it as a code pointer, not a data source.
